content.text: The Freedom Movement in Andhra: Mass Satyagrahas, Subaltern Resistance, Revolutionary Literature, and Linguistic Statehood

The nationalist awakening in Andhra was multifaceted, combining the pan-Indian anti-colonial struggle with the non-Brahmin socio-political assertion, epic tribal guerrilla warfare under Alluri Sitarama Raju, radical progressive literature, and the long agitation of the Andhra Mahasabha for linguistic self-determination that culminated in the martyrdom of Potti Sreeramulu and the creation of Andhra State in 1953 and Andhra Pradesh in 1956.
1. The Non-Brahmin Assertion & The Justice Party in Andhra

Formed in 1916 as the South Indian Liberal Federation (SILF / Justice Party) by Pitti Theagaraya Chetty, Dr. T.M. Nair, and the Raja of Panagal (P. Ramarayaningar), the movement contested Brahmin dominance over higher education, the bar, and provincial civil services:

items: Communal Representation: Under the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms (Government of India Act 1919), the Justice Party formed ministries in Madras Presidency (1920–1926 and 1930–1937). Prominent Andhra leaders included Kurma Venkata Reddy (K.V. Reddy) Naidu and A.P. Patro (Minister of Education).

Key Legislative Reforms: Enacted the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act 1926 (taking temple management out of private priestly hands), introduced communal quotas in public appointments (First Communal G.O. of 1921), and established Andhra University at Visakhapatnam in 1926 (piloted by A.P. Patro; C.R. Reddy served as its founding Vice-Chancellor).

Rationalist Literature: Tripuraneni Ramaswamy Choudhary (titled 'Kaviraju', 1887–1943) championed rationalist anti-orthodoxy through provocative Telugu literary dramas such as 'Suta Puranam', 'Sambhuka Vadha', and 'Kurukshetra Sangramam', celebrating subaltern and Dravidian characters.

content.text: 2. Major Gandhian Mass Campaigns in Andhra

content.caption: Milestone Nationalist Agitations in Andhra (1920–1942)
rows: Held on March 31 – April 1, 1921. Pingali Venkayya (from Bhatlapenumarru, Krishna district) presented his design of the National Flag (Red and Green bands) to Gandhi, who added white and the spinning charkha. Raised 1 crore rupees for Tilak Swaraj Fund.

Protesting forced conversion of Chirala-Perala villages into a municipality with 400% tax hikes, Duggirala organized the evacuation of all 15,000 residents to huts in adjacent 'Nagarampalem', establishing a parallel civic government defended by his volunteer corps ('Rama Dandu') for 11 months.

Total non-payment of land revenue; village officers (Karnams and Reddis) resigned en masse. Total administrative paralysis compelled the Madras Governor to deploy military forces; suspended following Gandhi's Bardoli resolution.

Peasants and cattle grazers defied oppressive colonial grazing taxes (Pullari taxes) by entering reserve forests. Police fired on villagers at Minchalapadu on February 26, 1922, martyring young leader Kanneganti Hanumanthu.

During the Simon Commission protest in Madras on February 3, 1928, police opened fire and shot a youth. When armed soldiers prevented access, Prakasam tore open his shirt and bared his chest, shouting 'Shoot me if you dare!', earning the immortal title 'Andhra Kesari' (Lion of Andhra).
Tanguturi Prakasam, Konda Venkatappayya, Kasinathuni Nageswara Rao

Satyagraha Sibirams (camps) established along coastal Andhra; major salt-making marches to Machilipatnam, Chinnaganjam, and Vadarevvu; widespread picketing of liquor and foreign cloth shops by women leaders like Duvvuri Subbamma.

content.text: 3. The Rampa Rebellion (1922–1924) & Alluri Sitarama Raju
The Manyam Rebellion (Rampa Revolt) represented South India's fiercest armed tribal guerrilla struggle against British colonialism, led by charismatic warrior-mystic Alluri Sitarama Raju (1897–1924):

items: Causes of Revolt: Oppressive implementation of the Madras Forest Act 1882, severely curtailing the tribal right to gather forest produce and practice Podu (slash-and-burn) agriculture; brutal forced unpaid labor (Vetti) extracted by colonial Tahsildar Bastian for constructing forest roads in Gudem agency.

Guerrilla Warfare: Raju mobilized the Koya and Konda Dora tribals, alongside lieutenants Gam Mallu Dora and Gam Gantam Dora. Using traditional bows alongside captured modern Lee-Enfield rifles, he conducted tactical raids on police stations at Chintapalli, Krishnadevipeta, Rajavommangi, Addateegala, and Rampachodavaram. Raju famously signed police station visitor books before each raid, daring the British to stop him.

British Counter-Insurgency: The British deployed the Assam Rifles, Malabar Special Police, and experienced counter-insurgency officers (Rutherford, Saunders, Tremenheere). Raju was eventually captured at Mampa and shot dead without trial at Koyyuru on May 7, 1924, by Major Goodall. He was cremated at Krishnadevipeta, remembered as 'Manyam Veerudu' (Hero of the Jungles).

content.text: 4. Nationalist, Dalit, and Progressive Telugu Literature

content.caption: Pioneering Nationalist and Subaltern Literary Titans of Andhra
rows: 'Maa Koddi Tella Doratanamu' (We don't want this white man's government)
Written during Non-Cooperation; sung across Andhra villages; so potent that British Collector Rutherford jailed Garimella for one year simply for singing it in public.
Pioneer of romantic-nationalist Telugu poetry (Bhavakavitvam); composed 'E desham egina endukan galidina, pogadara nee thalli bhoomi Bharatini'.
Epochal Telugu novel depicting Gandhian philosophy, Bolshevism, and Dalit empowerment; written while imprisoned in Vellore Jail; confiscated and banned twice by colonial authorities.
Titled 'Kavi Kokila'; 'Gabbilam' adapted Kalidasa's Meghaduta where an untouchable sends his tragic prayer of sorrow to Lord Shiva at Varanasi through a bat, laying bare caste untouchability.
Championed Ambedkarite consciousness; his drama 'Paleru' inspired thousands of Dalit farm-servants (Palerlu) to abandon bonded servitude and seek higher education.
Father of modern progressive Telugu poetry (Abhyudaya Kavitvam); championed the working class, toilers, and downtrodden ('Kammagani, Karukomali, Kannerolo, Karunarasam...').

content.text: 5. The Andhra Movement and the Genesis of Andhra State (1953) & Andhra Pradesh (1956)
The demand for an independent Telugu linguistic province gained momentum in the early 20th century:

items: Andhra Mahasabha: The First Andhra Conference convened at Bapatla in May 1913, presided by Bayya Narasimheswara Sarma, demanding a separate Andhra province from Madras Presidency. Subsequent conferences at Vijayawada (1914) and Visakhapatnam (1915) solidified public consensus under Konda Venkatappayya, Pattabhi Sitaramayya, and Mutnuri Krishna Rao.

The Sri Bagh Pact (November 14, 1937): Concluded at the Madras residence ('Sri Bagh') of K. Koti Reddy to resolve regional trust deficits between Coastal Andhra and Rayalaseema. Key terms: (1) Capital or High Court to be located in Rayalaseema; (2) Priority for irrigation and power projects to Rayalaseema from Krishna and Tungabhadra waters; (3) University centers at Visakhapatnam and Anantapur; (4) Equal legislative weightage.

Post-Independence Obstacles: The Dhar Commission (1948) and JVP Committee (1948; Nehru, Patel, Pattabhi) rejected the immediate reorganization of states on linguistic lines, arguing it threatened national unity.

Martyrdom of Amarajeevi Potti Sreeramulu (1952): Potti Sreeramulu undertook an uncompromising fast unto death starting on October 19, 1952, at Bulusu Sambamurti's house in Madras, demanding a separate Andhra state. After 58 heroic days of fasting, he attained martyrdom on the night of December 15, 1952. Riots and mass civil disobedience forced Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru to announce the formation of Andhra State.

Inauguration of Andhra State (October 1, 1953): Carved out of 11 Telugu districts of Madras Presidency with Kurnool as capital and Guntur as High Court (honoring the Sri Bagh Pact). Tanguturi Prakasam Pantulu took oath as first Chief Minister; C.M. Trivedi was appointed Governor; N. Sanjiva Reddy was Deputy Chief Minister.

Gentlemen's Agreement (February 20, 1956): Signed at Hyderabad House, New Delhi, between Andhra leaders (B. Gopala Reddy, N. Sanjiva Reddy, G. Latchanna, Alluri Satyanarayana Raju) and Telangana leaders (B. Ramakrishna Rao, K.V. Ranga Reddy, M. Chenna Reddy, J.V. Narsing Rao), guaranteeing safeguards on regional representation, cabinet parity, expenditure surplus allocation, and education quotas (Mulki rules).

Formation of Andhra Pradesh (November 1, 1956): The States Reorganisation Act 1956 merged the Andhra State with the Telugu-speaking Telangana districts of Hyderabad State to create Andhra Pradesh, with Hyderabad as its capital and Neelam Sanjiva Reddy as the first Chief Minister.

content.text: Part A: Mains Analytical & Descriptive Questions

items:
Analyze the origin, nature, and military course of the Rampa Tribal Rebellion (1922–1924) led by Alluri Sitarama Raju. Why did it evoke widespread popular sympathy? (APPSC Group-1 Mains, 10 Marks)
-> Model Approach: Introduce Alluri Sitarama Raju and the agency tracts of Eastern Ghats; detail systemic grievances (Madras Forest Act 1882 banning Podu farming, Muthadari police extortion, unpaid Vetti labor under Bastian); examine Raju's innovative military strategy (guerrilla ambushes, tactical raids on police stations for firearms, advance notice warnings); explain counter-insurgency deployment (Assam Rifles, Malabar police, Rutherford) leading to his martyrdom on May 7, 1924; evaluate his symbolic status as 'Manyam Veerudu' inspiring the broader national freedom movement.

Explain the historical significance of the Sri Bagh Pact (1937) in bringing about consensus between Coastal Andhra and Rayalaseema leaders. (APPSC Group-1 Mains, 10 Marks)
-> Model Approach: Contextualize Rayalaseema's anxieties regarding demographic domination, chronic drought, and resource allocation by coastal districts; outline the conference at Sri Bagh in November 1937; enumerate core compromises: choice of capital vs. high court, priority riparian rights over Krishna-Tungabhadra waters, and equitable educational investment; discuss its historical role in the establishment of Kurnool as the capital in 1953 and subsequent irrigation guarantees.

Examine the socio-literary impact of Dalit and progressive writers like Gurram Jashva, Unnava Lakshminarayana, and Sri Sri on Andhra society during the nationalist era. (APPSC Group-1 Mains, 10 Marks)
-> Model Approach: Analyze Unnava's 'Malapalli' as the pioneering Gandhian-Bolshevik social epic challenging bonded labor; evaluate Gurram Jashva's 'Gabbilam' as a searing poetic indictment of untouchability using classical meter; examine Sri Sri's 'Maha Prasthanam' as the revolutionary manifesto of the Abhyudaya movement, shifting poetic focus from feudal sentimentality to the working-class struggle.

content.text: Part B: Screening / Prelims Objective Questions

items:
Q1. At which historic session of the All India Congress Committee (AICC) in 1921 did Pingali Venkayya submit his design of the National Flag to Mahatma Gandhi?
(a) Kakinada Session
(b) Vijayawada Session
(c) Rajahmundry Session
(d) Guntur Session
Correct Answer: (b) Vijayawada Session [Explanation: On March 31 – April 1, 1921, during the AICC meeting at Vijayawada, Pingali Venkayya presented the flag design, to which Gandhi added white and the spinning wheel.]

Q2. Who led the famous Chirala-Perala non-cooperation struggle by organizing the entire population into a makeshift settlement named 'Nagarampalem'?
(a) Tanguturi Prakasam Pantulu
(b) Duggirala Gopalakrishnayya
(c) Konda Venkatappayya
(d) Parvataneni Veerayya Chowdary
Correct Answer: (b) Duggirala Gopalakrishnayya [Explanation: Duggirala Gopalakrishnayya ('Andhra Ratna') led the exodus of Chirala-Perala residents to Nagarampalem in 1921 supported by his Rama Dandu volunteers to protest municipal taxation.]

Q3. The famous nationalist song 'Maa Koddi Tella Doratanamu' (We don't want this white man's government) was composed by which Andhra poet?
(a) Rayaprolu Subbarao
(b) Garimella Satyanarayana
(c) Gurram Jashva
(d) Chilakamarti Lakshmi Narasimham
Correct Answer: (b) Garimella Satyanarayana [Explanation: Garimella Satyanarayana composed this song during the Non-Cooperation Movement, which spread like wildfire across Telugu villages and resulted in his imprisonment.]

Q4. On what date did Amarajeevi Potti Sreeramulu attain martyrdom after his 58-day fast unto death demanding a separate Andhra state?
(a) October 1, 1953
(b) November 1, 1956
(c) December 15, 1952
(d) January 26, 1950
Correct Answer: (c) December 15, 1952 [Explanation: Potti Sreeramulu began his fast on October 19, 1952, and breathed his last on the night of December 15, 1952, after 58 heroic days of fasting.]

Q5. Which famous classic Telugu novel, depicting the struggles of the Dalit rural community and banned twice by the British government, was authored by Unnava Lakshminarayana?
(a) Kanyasulkam
(b) Malapalli
(c) Rajasekhara Charitramu
(d) Maidanam
Correct Answer: (b) Malapalli [Explanation: Unnava Lakshminarayana wrote 'Malapalli' (Sangaradasu Katha) while incarcerated in Vellore Jail in 1922; it was banned by the colonial government for inciting rebellion and class solidarity.]
